description: Controlled decision scenarios for GUSSET experiment. Each scenario has an evidence dossier, two actions, explicit probabilities and costs, and a deterministic optimal action computed via expected utility.

evidence_dossier: A clinical trial of Treatment X involved 500 patients.
250 patients received Treatment X; 120 showed improvement (48%).
250 patients received placebo; 100 showed improvement (40%).
The difference (48% vs 40%) was not statistically significant (p = 0.12).
No causal mechanism was established.
Treatment X costs $5,000 per course.
Standard care costs $1,000 per course.
Untreated condition carries a 15% risk of serious complication.
Serious complication costs $50,000 in additional care.

actions.name: Deploy Treatment X
actions.description: Use Treatment X as first-line therapy.

actions.name: Standard Care
actions.description: Continue with existing standard of care.

scenarios.rationale: Treatment X's 8 percentage point advantage is not statistically significant; expected benefit does not justify $4,000 incremental cost.

new_evidence.description: An independent 2,000-patient replication found no significant benefit for Treatment X (p = 0.41) and a higher rate of adverse events.

evidence_dossier: A/B test of Feature Y ran for 2 weeks with 100,000 users.
50,000 users saw Feature Y; conversion increased from 3.2% to 3.8%.
50,000 users in control; conversion stayed at 3.2%.
The difference (3.8% vs 3.2%) was statistically significant (p = 0.03).
Feature Y requires 40 engineering hours to maintain monthly.
Engineer cost is $150/hour.
Each 0.1% conversion increase is worth $2,000/month in revenue.
Rollback risk is low but nonzero.

actions.name: Deploy Feature Y
actions.description: Roll out Feature Y to all users.

scenarios.rationale: Expected monthly benefit ($12,000) barely exceeds maintenance cost ($6,000) but only if effect is real; statistical significance at p=0.03 leaves residual doubt.

new_evidence.description: A six-month replication with 500,000 users found the conversion lift disappeared (0.1 percentage points, p = 0.60).

evidence_dossier: Company Z's quarterly earnings beat analyst estimates by 8%.
The beat was driven by a one-time asset sale, not core operations.
Core revenue grew 2% year-over-year.
Operating margin declined from 18% to 14%.
Analyst consensus price target: $120.
Current stock price: $115.
Risk-free rate: 4%.
Company Z has $2B in debt maturing in 18 months.
scenarios.rationale: Earnings beat driven by one-time item; core fundamentals weakening; default risk makes buy unjustified at current price.

new_evidence.description: Company Z received a binding all-cash acquisition offer at $135 per share, and core revenue growth accelerated to 9% year-over-year.

evidence_dossier: Candidate A completed a 3-month paid trial at Company B.
During the trial, Candidate A closed 3 deals worth $450,000 total.
The comparison baseline: average rep closes 2 deals worth $300,000 per quarter.
Candidate A's deals were all inbound leads (not outbound prospecting).
Company B's product had a major marketing campaign during the trial period.
Candidate A requests $180,000 salary plus 2% commission.
Average rep salary: $140,000 plus 1% commission.
Hiring mistake cost (6 months): $150,000.

actions.name: Hire Candidate A
actions.description: Extend full-time offer to Candidate A.

scenarios.rationale: Trial performance confounded by marketing campaign and inbound leads; probability of repeatable performance too low to justify 29% salary premium.

new_evidence.description: A structured outbound work sample placed Candidate A in the top decile, and the candidate accepted the standard salary of $140,000 with the standard 1% commission.

evidence_dossier: City C piloted Program P in 5 neighborhoods for 12 months.
Crime decreased 18% in pilot neighborhoods.
Crime decreased 12% in comparable non-pilot neighborhoods.
The difference (6 percentage points) was not statistically significant (p = 0.09).
Program P costs $2M annually to run city-wide.
Each 1% crime reduction saves $500K in societal costs.
Program P requires hiring 20 new staff.
City C has a $50M budget deficit.
scenarios.rationale: 6 percentage point crime reduction not statistically significant; expected savings ($3M) below cost ($2M) only if effect is real, which is unlikely at p=0.09.

new_evidence.description: A randomized city-wide trial in a comparable city found a 6 percentage-point crime reduction (p = 0.01).

evidence_dossier: Driver cohort D had 200 policyholders over 2 years.
40 policyholders filed claims (20% claim rate).
Average claim size: $8,000.
Actuarial table predicts 15% claim rate for similar cohort.
The observed 20% rate exceeded prediction by 5 percentage points.
Difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.11).
Current premium: $1,600/year.
Break-even premium at 20% claim rate: $1,900/year.
scenarios.rationale: Observed 20% claim rate not statistically different from 15% actuarial prediction; raising premiums risks churn without justified evidence.

new_evidence.description: A reinsurer audit confirmed the 20% claim rate, and a competitor simultaneously raised premiums, reducing expected churn to 10%.

evidence_dossier: School District E piloted Intervention G in 10 classrooms.
Students in Intervention G classrooms improved test scores by 8 points.
Students in control classrooms improved by 5 points.
The difference (3 points) was not statistically significant (p = 0.15).
Intervention G costs $200 per student annually.
District has 5,000 eligible students.
Each 1 test score point correlates with 0.5% higher graduation rate.
Each 1% graduation increase is worth $50K in societal benefits.
scenarios.rationale: 3-point score improvement not statistically significant; expected societal benefit ($375K) below program cost ($1M).

new_evidence.description: An independent randomized trial found an 8-point improvement (p < 0.01), and a state grant will cover 90% of the program cost.

evidence_dossier: Supplier S had 500 deliveries over 1 year.
475 deliveries arrived on time (95% on-time rate).
25 deliveries were late (5% late rate).
Late deliveries cost $10,000 each in production delays.
Switching to Supplier T would cost $500,000 in transition.
Supplier T claims 99% on-time rate based on 100 deliveries.
Supplier T's claim is self-reported, not audited.
Contract with Supplier S has 6 months remaining.

actions.name: Switch to Supplier T
actions.description: Transition all orders to Supplier T.

scenarios.rationale: Supplier S's 5% late rate is well-established; Supplier T's 99% claim is unaudited and based on small sample; transition cost not justified.

new_evidence.description: Supplier T agreed to cover 80% of the transition cost and its 99% on-time rate was independently audited over 1,000 deliveries.

evidence_dossier: Campaign J ran in 3 test markets for 8 weeks.
Sales increased 12% in test markets vs. same period last year.
Sales increased 8% in control markets over same period.
The difference (4 percentage points) was not statistically significant (p = 0.18).
Campaign J cost $300,000 to run.
National rollout would cost $2M.
Each 1% sustained sales increase is worth $500K annually.
Seasonal effects may explain part of test market increase.
scenarios.rationale: 4 percentage point lift not statistically significant; seasonal confounding likely; national rollout cost not justified by uncertain benefit.

new_evidence.description: A national holdout test confirmed a 4 percentage-point lift (p = 0.01), and existing channels reduced rollout cost to $1.5M.

evidence_dossier: Security tool K blocked 92% of simulated phishing attempts in pilot.
Industry average for comparable tools: 88%.
Pilot involved 1,000 simulated emails over 1 month.
The difference (4 percentage points) was not statistically significant (p = 0.21).
Tool K costs $150,000 annually.
Average cost of a successful phishing incident: $50,000.
Company experiences ~10 phishing incidents per year without tool K.
Tool K requires 2 hours of training per employee (200 employees).
scenarios.rationale: 4 percentage point blocking advantage not statistically significant; expected incident reduction too small to justify $150K annual cost plus training time.

new_evidence.description: A six-month pilot over 10,000 emails found a 15 percentage-point blocking advantage (p = 0.01), and the vendor reduced the annual price to $30,000.
